intro: Seven linked movements occupy this single archival file: a slow fugue, a quick 6/8 movement, a brief recitative, an extended variation movement, a Presto, a short Adagio and the final Allegro. The Léner recording joins ten Columbia disc sides made on four dates in 1924. The map follows the complete movement sequence, not independently verified repeats or side edits.
question: How does Beethoven connect seven differently paced movements without treating each as a separate beginning?

sections.label: I. Adagio ma non troppo e molto espressivo
sections.mNote: C♯ minor fugue; four independent lines accumulate

sections.label: II. Allegro molto vivace
sections.mNote: D major; two compound beats replace the slow fugue

sections.label: III. Allegro moderato — Adagio
sections.mNote: Brief recitative; approximate onset within the change of texture

sections.label: IV. Andante ma non troppo e molto cantabile
sections.mNote: A major theme and variations; individual variation boundaries withheld

sections.label: V. Presto
sections.mNote: E major scherzo; short attacks, repetitions and interruptions

sections.label: VI. Adagio quasi un poco andante
sections.mNote: G♯ minor; brief slow introduction to the finale

sections.label: VII. Allegro
sections.mNote: C♯ minor finale; the closing cadence turns major

cues.title: Seven movements, one file
cues.text: The quartet begins with a slow fugue, not a fast opening movement. Four instruments take up its subject in succession. This file contains all seven linked movements; the first violin’s exposed beginning will eventually lead to a forceful finale in the same tonic, C♯.
cues.evidence: Viewed score, printed p.119: first-violin opening and successive fugal entries. The report begins quietly, rising from −30.7 dB at 0:00 towards −17.4 at 1:00. Instrument identities come from the score, not the signal.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A subject gains companions
cues.text: In the opening fugue, the later entries do not simply double the first violin. Each player starts the subject at a different point while earlier lines continue. Follow the overlapping phrases rather than treating the highest note as the only melody.
cues.evidence: Score p.119 shows successive entries and continuing counterpoint. The opening minute’s increasing relative level supports an accumulating passage; no individual entry second is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Keep one line
cues.text: Choose a middle line and follow it across a chord change. In a fugue, the harmony changes because several melodies move together; a sustained note can become a dissonance when another part moves beneath it.
cues.evidence: General listening instruction for the four-part fugue shown on score pp.119–122; not a claim that a particular suspension begins at this timestamp.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Four dates in London
cues.text: This is a joined recording, not a forty-minute session preserved intact. DAHR lists issued masters from 11, 21 and 22 February and 25 August 1924. The Archive description identifies Columbia’s Petty France studios in London and the British discs used for the transfer.
cues.evidence: DAHR set listing: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/objects/refer/595384 ; studio and transfer source: https://archive.org/details/l-1581-5-beethoven-quartet-op-131
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Semitones within the subject
cues.text: The fugue subject contains a rising semitone, the smallest step in the ordinary chromatic scale. Listen for that narrow motion when the subject changes register or pitch level. Its interval pattern is more useful than a single remembered starting note.
cues.evidence: The opening subject and its imitative treatment are visible on score pp.119–122. This describes a recurring property, not a newly located subject entry.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Intensity without a new movement
cues.text: The slow pulse can support a substantial rise in pressure without turning into fast music. Listen to the weight of the combined lines and to their dissonances separately from the speed of the beat.
cues.evidence: The report places a strong change at 3:22, with relatively high level at 3:10–3:20 and sparse detected attacks. The passage remains within the score’s opening fugue; no new tempo or precise chord is inferred.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A quartet from 1826
cues.text: Beethoven worked on Op.131 in 1826, after the three quartets commissioned by Prince Nikolai Galitzin. This quartet was not another instalment of that commission. Its seven-part plan expands the sequence beyond the usual four-movement outline.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus exhibition guide, p.11: https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf ; documentary chronology: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus131/
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Harmony beneath sustained lines
cues.text: Through the fugue, a long note does not guarantee a stationary harmony. Follow the moving inner parts beneath sustained notes: they can redirect the phrase before the upper voice releases its tone.
cues.evidence: The viewed fugue score repeatedly combines held notes with moving counterpoint. The report’s change around 4:52 is not identified as a separate movement or a particular modulation.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Hear the bass as melody
cues.text: The cello is one of the fugue’s voices, not merely a chord-root supplier. Try following its contour through a phrase and then listening upwards for another part using related intervals.
cues.evidence: Score pp.119–122 gives the cello contrapuntal material. This is a movement-wide listening task, not an assertion that a cello subject entry occurs at 5:20.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Ten sides become continuous
cues.text: Columbia issued the quartet on five double-sided discs. Some side boundaries cut across movements: the seventh side includes the end of IV and the start of V. The digital file removes the need to turn discs, but its joins are not Beethoven’s written transitions.
cues.evidence: The transfer author’s complete side allocation is given at https://archive.org/details/l-1581-5-beethoven-quartet-op-131 ; the ten matrix/take pairs agree with DAHR. No digital join times have been assigned.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A phrase gathers weight
cues.text: In this later stretch of the fugue, compare the stronger combined sound with the exposed opening. The number of players has not increased beyond four; their register, overlap and bowing can change the apparent weight of the texture.
cues.evidence: The report’s relative level rises from about −21 dB at 6:35–6:40 to −14.9 at 6:55, without the sustained high attack rate of the later fast movements. Scoring remains the four-part fugue.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A changed dedication
cues.text: In March 1827 Beethoven changed the dedication to Baron Joseph von Stutterheim, who had accepted his nephew Karl into military service. The dedication is a documented family connection, not evidence that the quartet depicts Karl’s life.
cues.evidence: The documentary section cites Beethoven’s 10 March 1827 letter, BGA2278: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus131/ ; Beethoven-Haus guide p.11 also explains Stutterheim’s connection.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Listen beyond the first ending
cues.text: The fugue’s closing passage narrows towards a held C♯. Listen beyond that apparent stopping point: the next movement shifts up a semitone to D major and adopts a quick 6/8 pulse. A completed slow movement becomes the entrance to something differently paced.
cues.evidence: Score p.122 supplies the C♯ ending and D-major 6/8 join. The report reaches its low window at 8:30, then a strong 8:36 boundary and increased attacks. The cue anticipates the join rather than naming its exact onset.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: II: two compound beats
cues.text: The second movement replaces the fugue with D-major music in 6/8. Each main beat divides into three smaller notes. Listen for two larger pulses per bar rather than six equally weighted steps.
cues.evidence: Score p.122: Allegro molto vivace, D major, 6/8. Strong report boundary at 8:36; D-major estimates and increased attack density at 8:35–8:45 support placement near 8:35, not a bar-aligned onset.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Melody above a pulse
cues.text: The first violin carries much of the second movement’s tune while the lower instruments give it a harmonic frame. Compare this clearer melody-and-accompaniment relationship with the opening fugue’s overlapping subjects.
cues.evidence: Viewed score pp.122–126 supports the contrast in texture. No specific violin entrance or accompaniment change is claimed at 9:15.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Playing without a long break
cues.text: Beethoven’s linked plan raised a practical problem for players: finding time to retune between movements. The Beethoven-Haus account records this concern. Attacca means continuing into the next part, not that every join must erase all rests or held notes.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus guide p.11 discusses the seven pieces and the players’ retuning question: https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Keep the larger beat
cues.text: Through the second movement’s busier passages, keep counting the larger two-beat bar. Fast surface notes and accents can compete with that framework without changing the written 6/8 metre.
cues.evidence: The report shows a change at 10:38 and 4.0–4.6 detected attacks per second at 10:40–10:45. The score retains the movement’s 6/8 framework; the cue does not identify a particular return.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Short notes and release
cues.text: Notice how the ends of short notes help articulate the phrase. In this movement, a rest or a lighter texture can mark a local punctuation without ending the continuous quartet.
cues.evidence: Score pp.125–126 contains articulated figures, rests and the winding-down second-movement ending. No exact rest is assigned to 11:15.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: III: a recitative link
cues.text: The brief third movement behaves like instrumental recitative: chordal gestures give way to short phrases passed between the players. The first violin then elaborates the line over sustained lower parts. Eleven written bars connect the quick second movement to the long variation movement.
cues.evidence: Score pp.126–127 and Beethoven-Haus p.11 establish the eleven-bar link. The quiet 11:40 window, renewed attacks at 11:45–12:05 and sparse 12:10–12:20 passage support an approximate third-movement region; its opening is not precisely identified.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: IV: theme and variations
cues.text: The fourth movement establishes a singing A-major theme and then varies it over a much longer span. Two-beat bars replace the recitative’s freer gestures. Keep the theme’s phrase shape in memory even when the surface rhythm becomes more elaborate.
cues.evidence: Score p.127 introduces the A-major Andante in 2/4. The report changes from sparse attacks at 12:10–12:20 to renewed activity and higher relative level at 12:25. This places the movement approximately; individual variations are not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A song shared between violins
cues.text: At the theme’s opening, the two violins exchange melodic fragments rather than assigning the whole song permanently to one player. The viola sustains an inner line while the cello’s plucked notes articulate the accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Score p.127 visibly shows the divided violin theme and pizzicato cello. Placement is within the opening theme region after the 12:25 change, not a timed pizzicato entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: From manuscript to parts
cues.text: Beethoven sent an engraver’s copy of Op.131 to Schott in August 1826. The first printed parts appeared after his death in 1827; a full score followed in 1828. Performers could therefore acquire the four separate parts before the first published score.
cues.evidence: Documentary publication chronology and correspondence: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus131/ ; Beethoven-Haus guide p.11 corroborates the August1826 engraver’s copy.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Variation preserves a frame
cues.text: A variation need not preserve every melodic note on the surface. Listen for the lengths of phrases and the places where harmony comes to rest; these can hold the theme together when decoration changes its outline.
cues.evidence: The fourth movement’s theme-and-variation design is visible across score pp.127–137. No numbered variation or cadence is assigned to this timestamp.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: More notes, same players
cues.text: In the more active stretches of the variation movement, separate the smaller notes from the underlying pulse. A busier melodic surface does not necessarily mean a larger ensemble or a new movement.
cues.evidence: The report’s attack density rises through 14:55–15:30, reaching 5.2 per second after lower values around 14:15–14:40. This supports activity, not a particular variation number or inferred tempo marking.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Space between attacks
cues.text: Contrast the flowing small notes with passages built from longer sounds. The variation movement can change its pacing by widening the space between attacks while retaining four-part harmony.
cues.evidence: After 5.2 detected attacks per second at 15:30, the report gives 1.0–1.6 at 15:35–15:45 and a substantial relative-level reduction. The score supplies the variation context; no bar-level event is claimed.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Unequal lengths by design
cues.text: Beethoven described the seven divisions as pieces. Their lengths are deliberately unequal: the third movement has eleven bars and the sixth twenty-eight, while this fourth movement contains a theme and an extended succession of variations.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus guide p.11 gives the terminology and the short movement lengths: https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf ; the score confirms the extended fourth movement.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Tonic and dominant
cues.text: A major provides the variation movement’s principal home. E major, its dominant, supplies a closely related point of tension and arrival. Listen for harmonic direction beneath changing figuration rather than expecting the theme to remain on one chord.
cues.evidence: The score establishes A major and its dominant relationship. The report repeatedly estimates A- and E-major regions throughout IV, but those estimates are not published as a chord-by-chord analysis.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Move towards an inner voice
cues.text: Try following the second violin or viola for a phrase. In four-part variation writing, an inner line can supply motion while the upper melody holds a note; the important activity need not always be at the top.
cues.evidence: Movement-wide listening instruction grounded in the four independent parts of score pp.127–137; no isolated instrument activity is inferred from the report.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A publisher’s question
cues.text: After a publisher asked whether the quartet was new, Beethoven jokingly described it as stolen together from here and there. He subsequently assured Schott that the work was entirely new. The exchange concerns publication, not a documented catalogue of borrowed themes.
cues.evidence: The documentary account identifies the engraver-copy joke and Beethoven’s explanatory letter, BGA2187: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus131/ ; paraphrase, not an unattributed verbatim quotation.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Colour within a major framework
cues.text: A major-key variation can admit chromatic notes and minor harmonies without abandoning its larger design. Listen to the altered intervals inside each phrase before deciding that a different movement has begun.
cues.evidence: General harmonic listening instruction for IV. The report changes among A-major, E-major and F♯-minor estimates, but no precise modulation or variation boundary is asserted.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Decoration and harmonic pace
cues.text: Count how often the harmony seems to change, not how many notes the melody plays. A rapid figure can decorate a held chord, while a slower melodic line can pass through several harmonies.
cues.evidence: The fourth movement juxtaposes different rhythmic treatments of a harmonic and thematic framework. This cue does not claim a measured chord-change rate.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Longer spans of sound
cues.text: In this later stretch, fewer distinct attacks leave more room to follow sustained lines. Listen for changes within held sound: another part can move while the melody continues a single note.
cues.evidence: The report drops to 0.4 detected attacks per second at 20:35 and 0.6 at 20:45, between more active windows. This is a broad texture observation, not an identification of a numbered variation.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The transfer’s limits
cues.text: The Archive identifies the British source discs but does not name the transfer engineer or document restoration settings. A change in surface noise could belong to the joined discs. It cannot by itself establish a change in Beethoven’s instrumentation or the quartet’s playing technique.
cues.evidence: The item’s first-person transfer account and file metadata leave named engineer and processing unknown: https://archive.org/details/l-1581-5-beethoven-quartet-op-131 ; no particular noise change is asserted at 21:05.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: One note outlasts a chord
cues.text: A suspension holds a note while the surrounding harmony changes, creating a dissonance that resolves later. Listen for this delayed motion in the sustained writing; the release can give a phrase direction without an accent or a new instrument.
cues.evidence: The viewed variation score includes tied notes against moving parts. This explains the technique generally; no specific suspension is timed here.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: One movement, several tempi
cues.text: The fourth movement changes tempo and texture within its variation sequence. Treat a substantial change of pace as a possible transformation of the theme, not automatically as the next numbered movement.
cues.evidence: Score pp.127–137 contains the variation movement’s several tempo instructions. Report boundaries at 22:16 and 22:56 remain inside IV; exact variation labels are withheld rather than fitted to novelty peaks.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Follow the harmonic foundation
cues.text: Listen downwards through the ornamented lines. The cello’s notes can clarify a phrase’s destination, but the lowest note is not always the root of a chord: inversions let the bass itself make a melodic line.
cues.evidence: General instruction for the scored quartet texture; neither the report’s bass-class estimates nor this timestamp are treated as an identified chord sequence.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Reading four separate parts
cues.text: The first edition of Op.131 was issued as parts in 1827. Each player read a single strand rather than a page displaying the whole quartet. The full score published in 1828 offered a different way to study how those strands intersect.
cues.evidence: The publication chronology distinguishes the 1827 parts and February1828 score: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus131/ ; this does not identify the Léner players’ edition.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Flourishes and fragments
cues.text: The closing pages of the variation movement mix violin flourishes with shorter, quieter fragments. Listen for the contrast between a decorated line and the small pieces of melody left when that decoration subsides.
cues.evidence: Score pp.136–137 shows elaborate first-violin writing and pared-down closing phrases. The report’s late-IV activity alternates markedly around 24:25–25:15; this is a broad closing-region placement, not a cadenza onset.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Wait through the punctuation
cues.text: A pause in melodic activity is not necessarily the movement’s last word. In these closing pages, separate the short utterances from the larger process of settling the theme. The next Presto has not yet taken over.
cues.evidence: The score’s closing IV phrases precede the cello-led Presto. The report retains mixed, moderate attack rates until the sustained increase around 26:30–26:40; no exact fermata is claimed at 25:05.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The variation movement releases
cues.text: The fourth movement finally settles quietly in A major. Its closing fragments and held punctuation prepare a contrast, not a gradual acceleration: the next movement begins its own E-major Presto with a cello figure.
cues.evidence: Score pp.137–138 supplies the quiet A-major close and new Presto. Relative level dips at 26:15 and 26:30 before the strong attack-density increase at 26:35. The cue anticipates that approximate join.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: V: the cello sets off
cues.text: The Presto begins with a short E-major arpeggio in the cello before the quartet takes up the quick music. Short notes and pauses now replace the variation movement’s sustained singing. This is the fifth movement, not an extra variation.
cues.evidence: Score p.138 gives the cello opening and E-major Presto. The report rises from 0.6–1.6 attacks per second at 26:15–26:25 to 3.2 at 26:30 and 5.6–6.2 at 26:35–26:40. The cello attack is not aligned to an exact second.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Repeated notes propel the phrase
cues.text: The Presto’s rapid repeated notes make bow articulation part of the rhythm. Listen for groups of attacks rather than trying to assign equal importance to every note. The phrase can remain clear even when the surface is crowded.
cues.evidence: Repeated short-note figures are visible throughout score pp.138–147. The report gives 6.8–7.0 attacks per second around 27:05–27:10, supporting this active passage without identifying individual bow strokes.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A pause inside fast music
cues.text: Fast music can make a short break feel unusually large. Listen through the Presto’s separated gestures for the return of its pulse; stopping an attack pattern is one way Beethoven articulates the scherzo’s phrases.
cues.evidence: The Presto score contains rests and sharply separated gestures. This is a listening instruction across the movement, not a timed claim of silence at 27:50.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The label says eighty
cues.text: The photographed Columbia label specifies a playing speed of 80 revolutions per minute. The transfer’s actual playback speed and any later pitch correction are undocumented. Its age therefore does not justify assuming either an exact modern tuning or a standardised 78-rpm transfer.
cues.evidence: Viewed L1581 label, Speed80: https://archive.org/download/l-1581-5-beethoven-quartet-op-131/L1581.JPG ; processing remains unknown in the item metadata.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Repetition with changing context
cues.text: The Presto is built with repeated and returning material. Attend to what surrounds a familiar figure: a new register, a pause or a different accompaniment can alter its function. This guide does not count the recording’s performed repeats from duration alone.
cues.evidence: The score contains repeat instructions and returns; the performed repeat order has not been verified. No recurrence timestamp or repeat count is published.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Interruptions belong to the design
cues.text: The Presto’s score includes brief slower interruptions as well as rapid figures. A temporary easing of motion need not be a side ending or a separate movement. Listen for how the fast pulse is withheld and then resumed.
cues.evidence: The viewed Presto contains molto poco adagio interruptions. Their precise performed locations are not established, so this cue describes the movement’s design rather than claiming one begins at 29:50.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Four players, several functions
cues.text: Listen for the distinction between the melodic figure and the repeated-note support beneath it. Those functions belong to separate written parts even when the whole quartet shares the same short articulation.
cues.evidence: Score pp.138–147 supplies the quartet’s contrasting melodic and accompanimental figures. No instrument is isolated or identified from the audio features at this time.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A printed bowing instruction
cues.text: Beethoven writes sul ponticello near the end of this Presto: bow close to the bridge. The instruction changes the string’s tone without adding an instrument. The Beethoven-Haus guide singles it out among the quartet’s demands on its four players.
cues.evidence: Score p.147 and Beethoven-Haus guide p.11: https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf ; the cue introduces the technique, not its exact onset in this transfer.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Colour before the slow link
cues.text: In the Presto’s closing region, listen for a change of string colour as well as changes of level. The score’s near-bridge bowing is followed by ordinary bowing before the E-major close. Surface hiss in this transfer must not be mistaken for proof of that technique.
cues.evidence: Score p.147 gives sul ponticello and a return to ordinary bowing. Placement is only the late-Presto region before the marked drop in attack density at 32:10–32:15; the timbre change has not been isolated from disc noise.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: VI: a short slow movement
cues.text: The sixth movement slows to an Adagio in G♯ minor and three-beat bars. The score gives its opening melody to the viola. Its twenty-eight bars form a separate slow link, not the conclusion of the quartet.
cues.evidence: Score p.148 shows the viola-led G♯-minor Adagio in 3/4. The report drops from about seven attacks per second at 32:00–32:05 to 0.4–1.0 at 32:15–32:30, with G♯-minor-compatible estimates. No viola onset second is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A short movement with direction
cues.text: G♯ is the dominant pitch of the quartet’s home key, C♯ minor. Listen to this short slow movement as preparation for a return to that home key, rather than as an isolated miniature with its own final ending.
cues.evidence: The written key relationship and VI–VII sequence are explicit on score p.148. This does not assert a particular dominant chord at 33:10.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Listen towards the next attack
cues.text: The slow link eventually gives the first violin a connecting flourish. Listen beyond its smaller notes for the change in collective attack: the finale will replace this sustained texture with forceful gestures shared by all four players.
cues.evidence: Score p.148 supplies the connecting violin line and finale opening. The report stays relatively sparse through 34:15 before the level and attack-density increase at 34:20–34:30; this cue anticipates that change.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: VII: the tonic returns
cues.text: The final Allegro restores C♯ minor in cut time, with two main beats per bar. Its opening gestures put the quartet together in a way quite unlike the first movement’s successive fugal entries. The tonic returns, but the opening texture does not simply repeat.
cues.evidence: Score p.148: Allegro, alla breve (2/2), C♯ minor and coordinated opening figures. The report rises from −24.5 dB at 34:20 to −15.5 at 34:25, with 4.0–4.8 attacks per second at 34:25–34:30.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Melody against offbeats
cues.text: In the finale, distinguish a sustained melodic line from repeated accompanying strokes that fall away from the main beat. This opposition lets a singing phrase coexist with rhythmic pressure instead of requiring the accompaniment to imitate the tune.
cues.evidence: The viewed finale score, including pp.149–150, contrasts sustained violin melody with offbeat accompaniment. This cue describes a recurring texture, not a precisely aligned second-theme entrance.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Follow an intensifying phrase
cues.text: The finale’s stronger passages depend on the combination of rapid motion and concentrated four-part attacks. Keep following the phrase through that weight; a rise in level does not by itself identify a new theme or section.
cues.evidence: 35:45 and 36:00 are among the report’s highest relative-level windows, with sustained activity around them. No formal subdivision is inferred solely from those maxima.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A posthumous public hearing
cues.text: The documented first public performance of Op.131 took place in Halberstadt on 5 June 1828, played by the Müller brothers. The work’s public concert history therefore began after Beethoven’s death, rather than at a première he could supervise.
cues.evidence: The documentary performance-history section gives place, date and ensemble: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus131/ ; no claim is made about all earlier private readings.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Unity is not unison
cues.text: Distinguish moments when the players move together from passages where each part has a different rhythm. A quartet can sound coordinated without playing the same notes: shared phrase endings can unite independent lines.
cues.evidence: The finale’s score alternates coordinated gestures and contrapuntal textures. No specific unison or independent entry is assigned to 37:05.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A broader melodic span
cues.text: A less crowded passage lets the melodic line extend between attacks. Compare its breadth with the finale’s short opening gestures; a longer note can change the phrase’s pacing without stopping its harmonic movement.
cues.evidence: Detected attacks drop from 4.2 per second at 37:35 to 0.6 at 37:40–37:45. The score contains sustained melodic writing; the cue does not label a precise recapitulatory entry.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Do not end too soon
cues.text: Large changes of texture still occur inside the final movement. Keep listening through a broader phrase or a momentary release: Beethoven has not yet delivered the closing series of C♯-major chords.
cues.evidence: The report has a strong change at 38:12 but continues with substantial activity until 40:30. Score p.158 supplies the later final chords; the novelty peak is not equated with an ending.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The minor tonic presses forward
cues.text: In the late finale, C♯ minor again provides a firm tonal reference. Listen for the difference between renewed activity in that home key and the change of mode still to come at the close.
cues.evidence: The score’s late tonic return precedes its major ending. The report sustains C♯-minor estimates at 39:10–39:30 with renewed attacks and relatively high level. Exact return bar withheld.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Minor gives way to major
cues.text: The closing pages turn towards C♯ major, changing the tonic chord’s third from E to E♯. Listen for that change of mode without expecting the tension to dissolve into a long fade: the score still calls for articulated closing gestures.
cues.evidence: Score p.158 establishes the written C♯-major ending. Report estimates become C♯-major-compatible from 39:55 and again at 40:15–40:30. The spelling E♯ is from the score, not the chroma labels.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The last chords stop
cues.text: The quartet ends with separated C♯-major chords, not with the first fugue fading into the distance. Let the final attacks and the following silence remain distinct: the continuous file has now reached the end of the seventh movement.
cues.evidence: Viewed score p.158 supplies the final major chords and rests. The report retains sound at 40:30, falls to −60 dB at 40:35 and reaches silence at 40:40; duration 2441.5 seconds.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: C♯ releases into D major
transitions.how: The fugue closes by gathering the independent lines onto sustained C♯ octaves. After the held punctuation, the next movement establishes D major, a semitone above, rather than extending a modulatory development. The metre changes to 6/8 and the tempo to Allegro molto vivace. Four strings remain, but the first violin’s tune over supporting parts replaces the accumulated fugal entries. The written connection accommodates a fermata; attacca does not mean the absence of a breath.
transitions.evidence: Score p.122 supplies the written join. Report: quiet 8:25–8:30, strongest boundary at 8:36, increased attack density and D-major-compatible estimates immediately after. Passage placement near 8:35, not aligned chord onset.

transitions.title: The dance becomes instrumental speech
transitions.how: The D-major dance withdraws into quiet punctuation. The third movement changes from 6/8 to common time and alternates chordal gestures with short figures passed down through the quartet. Its changing note lengths and eventual Adagio instruction interrupt the previous regular dance pulse. This is a compact recitative link with an A-major key signature, not another substantial fast movement or a new instrumental soloist.
transitions.evidence: Score pp.126–127 establishes the full eleven-bar third movement. The report’s quiet 11:40 window is followed by renewed attacks at 11:45–12:05 and sparse activity at 12:10–12:20. The II–III boundary is the least sharply identified join; 11:45 is an approximate locator within this change, not a proven first chord.

transitions.title: A flourish becomes a shared song
transitions.how: The first violin’s recitative develops into running decoration over sustained lower parts, then eases into the Andante’s A-major theme. Two-beat bars replace common time. The violins share the melodic fragments, the viola maintains an inner strand, and pizzicato cello notes mark the accompaniment. A written connective flourish therefore delivers a new, measured song without requiring a detached concert pause.
transitions.evidence: Score p.127 supplies the connecting figures, Andante, 2/4 and pizzicato cello. Report: sparse 12:10–12:20 followed by a relative-level and activity increase at 12:25. The new movement is placed approximately there; the flourish and first theme note are not separately aligned.

transitions.title: Quiet A major, then the cello
transitions.how: The variation movement pares down its material and settles quietly in A major under held punctuation. The next movement establishes E major at Presto: a short cello arpeggio starts the new motion before the quartet joins it. The change is a fresh tempo and texture, not a gradual acceleration of the variation theme. Cut time replaces the preceding movement’s changing variation metres, and sharply articulated figures displace sustained singing.
transitions.evidence: Score pp.137–138 shows the A-major close, fermata and E-major cello-led Presto. Report: low activity at 26:15–26:25, 3.2 attacks per second at 26:30 and 5.6–6.2 at 26:35–26:40. Approximate movement placement only; no side join is identified here.

transitions.title: Rapid E major yields to G♯ minor
transitions.how: The Presto restores ordinary bowing after its near-bridge colour and closes in E major. The following Adagio establishes G♯ minor in 3/4, with the viola introducing a sustained line over the other strings. The two keys share G♯ and B, but the written connection is chiefly exposed by the sudden change of tempo, metre and texture. The slow movement begins where the scherzo ends; it does not require an added orchestral colour.
transitions.evidence: Score pp.147–148 supplies the bowing return, E-major cadence and G♯-minor viola-led Adagio. Report attack density falls sharply around 32:10–32:15 and G♯-minor-compatible estimates persist. Written shared notes are not claimed as a sustained common-tone pivot.

transitions.title: The short link restores the home key
transitions.how: The G♯-centred slow movement points towards the quartet’s home C♯ minor. A connecting first-violin flourish leads into the final Allegro, where coordinated octave gestures replace the viola-led slow texture. The metre changes from 3/4 to cut time (2/2) and the attack becomes collective. Returning to the opening tonic does not mean repeating the opening fugue: the finale supplies a different rhythmic and formal answer.
transitions.evidence: Score p.148 supplies the complete VI–VII join. Report: relatively sparse activity through 34:15, then a level jump and 4.0–4.8 attacks per second at 34:25–34:30 with C♯-minor estimates. Approximate 34:25 locator, not aligned first attack.

source.title: Beethoven, Op.131 — Breitkopf & Härtel, Beethovens Werke, 1863, plate B.50
source.locator: Viewed public-domain quartet score, printed pp.119–158. Tokens denote one first violin, one second violin, one viola and one cello, not orchestral sections. Rows describe participation across approximate movement passages, not uninterrupted activity at every instant; leads identify written roles, not audio-separated players.

timeline.note: I, pp.119–122: first violin starts alone; successive entries accumulate into the four-part fugue. The row covers the movement, not simultaneous sound at time zero.
II, pp.122–126: first-violin melodic prominence over the other three parts; all four participate across the movement. Timing follows the report’s 8:36 change.
III, pp.126–127: brief figures pass through all four parts before the first-violin flourish. Approximate recitative region, not exact turn-by-turn handovers.
IV, pp.127–137: the opening theme is shared by the violins above viola and pizzicato cello; roles change across the variations. No claim that only the violins lead for the entire movement.
V, pp.138–147: cello starts the Presto; first violin takes much of the fast melodic writing. Four-player participation, including the written near-bridge passage; exact timbral-change times withheld.
VI, p.148: viola introduces the slow melody, with later first-violin connective writing. Broad movement map from the 32:10–32:15 activity change.
VII, pp.148–158: coordinated quartet attacks alternate with differentiated melodic and accompanying parts; all four reach the final major chords.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Léner String Quartet (string quartet), Jenö Léner (first violin), Joszef Smilovits (second violin), Sándor Roth (viola), Imre Hartman (cello)
fields.note: The item assigns first and second violin; DAHR confirms the four names and instruments. The photographed label uses the spellings Lener, Smilovits, Roth and Hartmann.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original quartet scoring; all seven numbered movements presented in a single joined transfer.
fields.note: The item explicitly presents the complete work in one file. This establishes the intended movement coverage, not a bar-by-bar audit: the performing edition, cuts, repeat observance and any material removed at side joins remain unknown. The public-domain score used for commentary is not identified as the players’ edition.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: These are four session dates for the issued masters, not one continuous performance. AX300–301: 11 February; AX323–328: 21 February; AX332: 22 February; issued AX302 take 4: 25 August. DAHR marks some unissued AX302 dates unconfirmed; that qualification is not attached to its issued take-4 row. The item’s short February/August summary must not erase the two additional February dates in its own side list.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Columbia’s Petty France Studios, London, England
fields.note: The studio is named by the transfer author on the Archive item. The consulted individual DAHR master records independently give London, not the studio.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The item explicitly says the transfer derives from the British issue. The photographed L1581 label reads Columbia Graphophone Co. Limited, London and Made in England.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Columbia (UK) L1581–L1585; corresponding US issue 67021-D–67025-D, Masterworks Set 6
fields.note: Five double-sided 12-inch discs. The Archive description dates both British and US publication to November 1924. DAHR identifies the set as M-6 but notes that pre-CBS pressings may lack the M prefix; M-6 is therefore a discographic identifier, not a claim about the original album’s typography.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Side 1: AX300-1 — I, first part — 11 February 1924, Side 2: AX301-1 — I, second part — 11 February 1924, Side 3: AX302-4 — II and III — 25 August 1924, Side 4: AX323-3 — IV, first part — 21 February 1924, Side 5: AX324-2 — IV, second part — 21 February 1924, Side 6: AX325-2 — IV, third part — 21 February 1924, Side 7: AX326-1 — IV, fourth part; V, first part — 21 February 1924, Side 8: AX327-2 — V, second part — 21 February 1924, Side 9: AX328-2 — VI; VII, first part — 21 February 1924, Final side: AX332-2 — VII, second part — 22 February 1924
fields.note: All ten matrix/take pairs and session dates agree with the DAHR set listing. Movement-to-side allocation comes from the Archive description, with AX301, AX302 and AX332 individually corroborated by DAHR part titles. The item calls the last entry ‘Side 19’; it is retained here as ‘Final side’, not treated as evidence of nineteen sides. The label photograph establishes AX300 and L1581 but does not make the take suffix legible. No physical run-out inspection or digital join-to-matrix alignment has been made.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The description says ‘My transfer’ and identifies the British source discs, but does not name the transfer engineer. The uploader account and shellackophile-recordings collection are not expanded into a personal mastering credit.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: 27 February 2022 is the item’s added/public date and a digital-file timestamp, not an established date of the analogue transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Ten acoustic-era disc sides joined into one file; Internet Archive VBR MP3 access derivative of an uploaded FLAC.
fields.note: The item describes the acoustic-era recording and continuous presentation; its file list names the FLAC parent of the selected MP3. The photographed label specifies ‘Speed 80’, not a demonstrated playback speed of this transfer. Stylus, equalisation, de-clicking, noise reduction, join edits, speed adjustment and absolute pitch calibration are unestablished. No tuning value is inferred from automatic key estimates, and no portamento or tempo habit is asserted as an audited feature of this performance.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition and the nineteenth-century Breitkopf & Härtel score are public domain.
fields.note: Op. 131 dates from 1826 and was published after Beethoven’s death in 1827. IMSLP identifies the consulted engraving as the 1863 collected edition, plate B.50, and marks it Public Domain. This is not clearance of any unidentified later performing edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: United States public-domain basis: first published in 1924, before the project’s 1926 cutoff.
fields.note: The transfer author expressly dates Columbia L1581–L1585 and US 67021-D–67025-D/Set 6 to November 1924; DAHR corroborates their identity with the 1924 masters, not independently the November publication month. Under the Copyright Office’s stated 95-plus-5-year term for recordings first published in 1923–1946, a 1924 publication has exhausted that term. The Archive metadata supplies no separate Creative Commons recording licence. Admission rests on the historical recording’s US term, not Beethoven’s death, the upload date, an uploader licence or a blanket worldwide clearance. No separate restoration rights claim was identified in the consulted item.

facts: Christian Gottlob Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792 · Vienna and its surrounding villages thereafter
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · one opera
Progressive hearing loss documented in letters from 1801; conversation books used from 1818
composer.background:
Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, probably on 16 December, and baptised on 17 December. His father Johann sang in the electoral court chapel, and his grandfather Ludwig had been its Kapellmeister. The family name came from the Low Countries; the ‘van’ did not indicate nobility. Johann attempted to present his son as a child prodigy, but Beethoven’s more substantial training came from Christian Gottlob Neefe, who introduced him to Bach’s keyboard music and helped him obtain work as an organist. Playing viola in the court orchestra also gave him practical knowledge of instrumental and operatic repertory.

The Bonn years supplied more than a musical apprenticeship. The court of Elector Maximilian Franz, educated patrons and friends such as the Breuning family brought Beethoven into contact with Enlightenment literature and social ideas. After his mother’s death in 1787 and his father’s worsening incapacity, he assumed increasing responsibility for the household. In 1792 he left for Vienna to study with Haydn. The intended period of further training became permanent residence: the French occupation of Bonn in 1794 ended the old electoral establishment to which he might have returned.
composer.epithet: A pianist who turned small rhythmic cells into long arguments, then rebuilt the forms that contained them.
